quantity.quote: The OPAL detector was about 12 m long, 12m high and 12m wide.
Currently the collaboration consists of about 200 physicists from 34 institutes in Canada, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Israel, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States.

name: OPAL
notes: 'OPAL' is expanded as 'Omni Purpose Apparatus for LEP' by INSPIRE (src:opal-inspire-experiment-record) and as 'an Omni-Purpose Apparatus at LEP' by OPAL's own collaboration site (src:opal-collaboration-site); both wordings are kept as aliases.

Unlike ALEPH (Point 4, CERN Courier) and DELPHI (Point 8, inferred via the LHCb/DELPHI shared-cavern story) and L3 (Point 2, inferred via the ALICE/L3 magnet story), no fetched source in this session states which LEP interaction point hosted OPAL. home.cern's own OPAL and LEP-collider pages, the OPAL collaboration site and detector-tour page, and the CERN Courier OPAL article (404, unreachable) were all checked; none gives a point number. By elimination among the ring's four instrumented points (2, 4, 6, 8) OPAL would be at Point 6, but that is not independently sourced, so no site is recorded for OPAL and none should be inferred from this note.

physics_goals.locator: 'The OPAL detector at LEP', Nucl.Instrum.Meth.A 305 (1991) 275, abstract
physics_goals.quote: The OPAL detector at the e+e- storage ring LEP is designed to provide precise measurements of charged particles and electromagnetic energy.
physics_goals.value: Measure charged particles and electromagnetic energy precisely across (almost) the full solid angle as a general-purpose LEP detector

summary.plain: One of four giant detectors on CERN's LEP electron-positron collider from 1989 to 2000, built as a layered, general-purpose apparatus about the size of a house to catch every kind of particle from the collisions.
summary.technical: General-purpose LEP detector, roughly 12 m × 12 m × 12 m, with tracking detectors, calorimeters and muon detectors arranged in concentric layers ('like the layers of an onion') around the beam pipe. Approved by the CERN LEPC on 18 November 1982; ran from August 1989 to 2 November 2000 with about 200 physicists from 34 institutes in 8 countries.

unique_capabilities.quote: The components of the detector were arranged outside the beam pipe, in a layered structure, rather like the layers of an onion.
unique_capabilities.value: A layered, 'onion-like' general-purpose design combining tracking, calorimetry and muon detection in concentric shells around the beam pipe
